questions.question: What is the difference between the DOM and the CSSOM?
questions.title: DOM versus CSSOM
questions.direct_answer: The DOM represents a document's content and element structure, while the CSSOM represents the parsed style rules that can apply to that document. A browser combines information from both when it decides what to render.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the two browser trees used during rendering.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating the DOM and CSSOM as one tree, or assuming hidden DOM nodes always appear in the render tree.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The DOM can contain nodes that are not rendered, and computed styles are the resolved result rather than a copy of one CSS rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The DOM is built from document markup and exposes document nodes.
The CSSOM is built from stylesheets and exposes CSS rules and resolved styles.
The browser uses both structures to calculate the visible render tree.
A DOM node may exist without producing a rendered box.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- The DOM and CSSOM are separate browser models. The DOM represents the document as nodes such as elements and text, while the CSSOM represents the style rules parsed from stylesheets. - During rendering, the browser matches CSS rules to DOM elements, resolves their computed styles, and uses the visible results to build a render tree. That render tree is then used for layout and paint. - For example, a `

` is a DOM element, and `.note { display: none; }` is represented through the CSSOM. The paragraph remains in the DOM, but it does not create a visible box in the render tree. - JavaScript can change either side: DOM APIs can add a class or node, and CSSOM-related APIs can inspect or modify styles. A change may cause style calculation, layout, or paint, but the exact work depends on what changed. - In short, the DOM answers “what is in the document,” the CSSOM answers “which styles apply,” and rendering turns those answers into pixels.

sections.title: Two models with different jobs
sections.content: HTML parsing produces a logical node tree. CSS parsing produces a rule model. Keeping those jobs separate explains why changing a class can alter the screen without creating a new DOM node, and why an element can still be found by JavaScript even when CSS prevents it from being displayed.

sections.title: How they meet during rendering
sections.content: Style calculation matches selectors against elements and resolves inherited, cascaded, and default values. The browser then keeps the parts needed for visual output and calculates geometry during layout. Pseudo-elements can create rendered content even though they are not ordinary DOM children, while metadata and `display: none` subtrees can remain outside the render tree. Developer tools expose these layers through the Elements, Styles, Computed, and Rendering panels.

sections.title: From source to pixels
sections.content:
HTML → DOM ───────────────┐
                            ├→ style calculation → render tree → layout → paint
CSS  → parsed style rules ─┘

sections.title: Observe structure and resolved style
sections.content:
```javascript
const note = document.querySelector('.note');
console.log(note instanceof Element); // true: it is in the DOM
console.log(getComputedStyle(note).display); // "none" when the rule applies
```
The element still exists even when it produces no visible box.

questions.question: How do NodeList and HTMLCollection differ?
questions.title: NodeList versus HTMLCollection
questions.direct_answer: An HTMLCollection contains elements and is usually live, so it reflects later DOM changes. A NodeList contains nodes; whether it is live depends on the API, and the NodeList returned by querySelectorAll() is static.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of collection type, liveness, and safe iteration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming every DOM collection is a fixed array or that every NodeList behaves the same way.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The producing API defines liveness; converting with Array.from() creates a snapshot but does not clone the nodes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: HTMLCollection contains only elements and is generally live.
NodeList can contain different node types, depending on the API.
querySelectorAll() returns a static NodeList; childNodes returns a live one.
Array.from(collection) gives a stable array snapshot of the references.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- NodeList and HTMLCollection are array-like DOM collections, but they are not ordinary arrays and they do not have identical rules. An HTMLCollection contains elements, whereas a NodeList can represent nodes such as elements and text nodes.

- The important difference is liveness. Collections such as `element.children` update as matching children are added or removed, while `document.querySelectorAll()` returns a static NodeList that keeps the members found when the query ran.

- For example, if a list has two `<li>` elements, `list.children` reports three immediately after another item is appended. A NodeList saved from `list.querySelectorAll('li')` still reports two until the selector is run again.

- A live collection can be useful when current membership is required, but changing the DOM while iterating it can skip or revisit elements because indexes move. `Array.from(collection)` creates a stable array of node references for predictable iteration.

- The safe rule is to check which API produced the collection instead of deciding from the type name alone.

sections.title: A collection is a view of nodes
sections.content: DOM collection objects expose indexed entries and a length, but their source remains the document tree. A live view reads current membership from that tree; a static view records membership at query time. Neither form copies the actual nodes, so changing a node through either reference still changes the document.

sections.title: Why liveness changes a loop
sections.content: Imagine removing the first child from a live collection on every pass. The former second child moves to index zero as soon as the tree changes. A loop that also increments its index may now jump over it. A static snapshot avoids membership changes during the loop, although removed node objects can still remain referenced in the snapshot until the array is released.

sections.title: Collection behaviour
sections.content:
| Source | Result | Contents | Membership |
|---|---|---|---|
| `element.children` | HTMLCollection | Elements | Live |
| `element.childNodes` | NodeList | All child nodes | Live |
| `querySelectorAll()` | NodeList | Matching elements | Static |
| `Array.from(collection)` | Array | Copied references | Static snapshot |
